text: It is not your imagination. Your credit card fees and interest rates are going up. Federal legislation limiting those fees doesn't go into effect until next February. So between now and then, banks and credit card companies are raising rates on a lot of customers.
John Ulzheimer is tracking the changes for Credit.com, that's a consumer site, and he joins us from the studios of Georgia Public Broadcasting in Atlanta.
Now, I understand that Citi has raised rates on some cards as high as 30 percent. How many other banks are doing the same thing?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: Citi is one of many credit card issuers who are changing their terms of a large portion of their cardholder accounts to be a little bit more favorable to the bank and less favorable to the consumer. We've seen this really across the board with most of the top 10 and top 15 credit card issuers. You know, the guys that everybody recognizes because they're the ones that, you know, we all have their cards in our wallet.
Yeah, like Chase, Capital One, Discover.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: You got it: Chase, Capital One, Discover, Bank of America, and pretty much anybody that's a well-known credit card issuer is going through some sort of process where they're changing the terms of our accounts in such a way that makes it more expensive for us to have their cards.
What else are they doing besides raising interest rates?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: It's the trifecta, is actually what we're calling it. It's the raising of the interest rates. It's the lowering of the credit limits, and it's the raising of the minimum payment requirements. And a lot of these things are happening in concert, which actually makes it difficult for some consumers to be able to make their payments on time. And in some cases, it's pushing them into default and having an adverse effect on their credit.
So what is the explanation on the part of the companies?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: That's an interesting question. The explanation that we're getting back varies, depending on who we're talking to and what issuer we're talking to. We're hearing some issuers state that the economy is to blame for their changes. And we're hearing some issuers state that it's the new legislation that's coming down the road in February of 2010 that's causing them to make these changes proactively, when they're still allowed to do so pretty much for any reason.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: We're also hearing from some issuers that are stating that their cardholder base is becoming more risky, and so that they're making these changes in order to compensate for the downside risk of many of their cardholders.

Now, doesn't this kind of violate the spirit of the law, in that they're - the law says that these companies aren't allowed to raise rates exorbitantly? And they're going ahead and doing it before the law takes effect. I imagine some people on Capitol Hill aren't too happy about that.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: No, and the people on Capitol Hill certainly aren't happy. Consumers certainly aren't happy. And then the watchdog groups are also certainly not happy. But, you know, with all due respect, we all expected this to happen. There is this pocket of time between when the president signs the Card Act and when it becomes enforceable law, and that's a one-year period. And we knew that the credit card issuers were going to finish their proactive housekeeping before it actually became more difficult for them to do so.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: So no one likes what they're doing, but it's certainly not illegal what they're doing. Is it immoral, unethical? I mean those are up for debate, certainly. And more consumers are finding themselves becoming the victim of some of these practices.
So what can we, consumers, do in the face of all this? Is there a way to avoid these high rates?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: Absolutely. There are a variety of ways, and I'm going to give you a few examples. First, vote with your wallet; take your business elsewhere if you don't like how your credit card issuer is treating you. Second, maintain very, very strong credit reports and very, very strong credit scores and you find yourself somewhat immune to what's going on in the credit environment right now.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: And last but certainly not least, be very, very selective about where you use your credit card. Be very conscientious of the fact that you issuer sees where you're shopping and sees the patterns that you're exhibiting. So avoid cash advances and avoid using your credit cards at what are referred to as questionable merchants, places like pawn shops, tire retreading stores, massage parlors, marriage counseling. Things like that are going to set off a red flag.
And you don't have to stick with the big guys. You can go with the small banks or the credit unions.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: Absolutely. Credit unions are not doing these things to consumers. They didn't need a Card Act to teach them and mandate how they treat customers properly. There are over 10,000 credit card issuers in this country and we tend to focus just on the top 10 or 15. Take your business elsewhere if you don't like how you're being treated.
John Ulzheimer is the president of Consumer Education at Credit.com.
Thanks.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (President, Consumer Education, Credit.com)
text: It was a pleasure.
From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Robert Siegel.
And I'm Michele Norris.

The implementation of the so-called Card Act two months ago was supposed to protect consumers from all kinds of onerous practices in the credit card industry. Under the law, companies would have a harder time raising rates or imposing fees. But there are worries that the legislation may have produced unintended side effects.
To talk about that, we're joined once again by John Ulzheimer. He's a credit expert with Credit.com. Welcome back to the program.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: Thank you so much for having me back.

Now, it was supposed to be harder for credit card companies to raise rates. But since February, when the Card Act took effect, some credit card customers are finding that they're actually paying higher rates. Why is this happening?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: Well, that's one of the great myths of the Card Act was that it was going to help protect consumers from higher interest rates. In fact, the Card Act does not prevent credit card issuers from increasing interest rates. It only requires that they provide a 45-day notice of the increase and the opportunity for the cardholder to opt out.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: The problem is, is that most consumers do not read the notices they receive in the mail from their credit card issuers, and so they sacrifice their rights after that 45-day period and they end up with a higher interest rate.
Hmm, so note to our listeners: Pay attention to the language, to the fine print in those bills that arrive at your home.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: That is exactly right. And a lot of these notices, Michele, are sent separately in innocuous white envelopes. And most of those end up in the shredder or in the garbage and that's where the notices are.
Companies, right now, are issuing fewer cards overall. According to one study, there's been a 50 percent drop. So where are the companies focused now to remain profitable?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: Well, right now, they are kind of recouping their goods, if you will, after the Card Act. And the target market today is the low risk market, so we're talking consumers who have very, very strong credit reports. They're not necessarily the most profitable cardholders because they're not going to pay 19 and 24 and 29 percent interest rates, but you will get your payment every single month, they will use the card. And that's where they're concentrating on building back their post-Card Act base of cardholders.
Are they running hard after those customers?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: They are absolutely running very hard after those customers. Everybody wants them right now because of this massive flight to quality. People who have very, very good credit scores are seeing their mailboxes fill up now for the first time in a very long time with offers from pretty much every major credit card issuer that you can name.

So there are certain customers that they're going after. There are other customers that they're trying to shed. Jamie Dimon in his annual shareholder letter yesterday, noted that his company, Chase, is planning to issue fewer credit cards. Some other companies - American Express, for example - paid some of its customers to basically close their accounts and go away. So who is considered to be somewhat toxic in terms of risk?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: Right now, the toxic cardholders - and this is almost comical -is the same cardholder that 36 months ago was the target cardholder: The consumer who has mediocre credit, maxes their card out, pays late. This a very, very risky cardholder. However, it's also a very, very profitable cardholder because they're paying interest income and they're paying late fees or over limit fees. So those are the folks who are seeing their cards closed.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: And you're right. Some - for example, American Express paid $300 to some of their cardholders to simply close the account. Other card issuers were not quite so kind and they just closed the account down. Incidentally, just to let you know, that does not require a 45-day notice or opt-out. You find out, frankly, when you go to use your card somewhere and it's declined.
It sounds like the credit card companies overall are spending a lot more time examining their consumer base and making all kinds of assumptions and coming to all kinds of conclusions about them.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: I think that's a very, very valid point and a very adept observation. And it's not as if they didn't pay attention prior to the Card Act or prior to the credit crunch. But I think today, they recognize that the safety net known as home equity just simply doesn't exist just yet. And so, truly it is now an unsecured product with really no safety net. So what they have to do is the assessment of credit risk must taken so much more seriously in today's environment than it was ever taken in the past.
John Ulzheimer, always good to talk to you. Thank so much.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN ULZHEIMER (Credit Score and Report Export, Consumer Education Credit.com)
text: It is always my pleasure.
John Ulzheimer is a credit expert with Credit.com.
